passages.text: Compromised item detection: A Bayesian change-point perspective
Abstract

Psychometric methods for accurate and timely detection of item compromise have been a long-standing topic. While Bayesian methods can incorporate prior knowledge or expert inputs as additional information for item compromise detection, they have not been employed in item compromise detection itself. The current study proposes a two-phase Bayesian change-point framework for both stationary and real-time detection of changes in each item's compromise status. In Phase I, a stationary Bayesian change-point model for compromise detection is fitted to the observed responses over a specified time-frame. The model produces parameter estimates for the change-point of each item from uncompromised to compromised, as well as structural parameters accounting for the post-change response distribution. Using the post-change model identified in Phase I, the Shiryaev procedure for sequential testing is employed in Phase II for real-time monitoring of item compromise. The proposed methods are evaluated in terms of parameter recovery, detection accuracy, and detection efficiency under various simulation conditions and in a real data example. The proposed method also showed superior detection accuracy and efficiency compared to the cumulative sum procedure.
INTRODUCTION

Continuous testing with repeated item usage is susceptible to item compromise. When an item is improperly distributed beyond its valid usage and no longer retains its original performance, the item is said to be compromised (Zara, ). Examinees who have gained unwarranted access to this item are examinees with item pre-knowledge, which may allow these examinees to correctly answer the compromised item with higher probability than their ability permits. For this reason, pre-knowledge and item compromise may considerably impair test security and the validity of the interpretation and use of test scores.

Various methods and techniques have been proposed to strengthen test security. From the standpoint of items, test security can be reinforced by either preventing test items from being overexposed or detecting them as soon as possible once they become compromised. As the focus of this paper is on detecting compromised items, we only review detection methods below for brevity. Interested readers may refer to Georgiadou et al.  for a relatively comprehensive review of prevention methods.

Compromised item detection can be implemented based on either static response data or responses collected on-the-fly during continuous test administration. In the statistical quality control (SQC) and change-point literature (e.g., Hawkins et al., ; Montgomery, ; Sinharay, ; Woodall & Montgomery, ), these applications are referred to as Phase I and Phase II problems, respectively. Phase I problems are finite-horizon problems where a large amount of data is first aggregated and the SQC analysis is applied only once to these aggregated data. Conversely, Phase II problems are infinite-horizon problems where the data stream is endless and the process is monitored on an ongoing basis.

Among the existing item compromise detection methods, the residual method in Wang and Liu  typifies Phase I detection where response data from one test administration were gathered; the observed correct response proportion on an item is compared with the model-implied values in the null distribution. However, this method is only able to report the resultant state of an item, compromised or not compromised. Other critical questions related to detection efficiency, such as when an item becomes compromised or how long the detection lag is, cannot be answered by this method.

Being aware that detection accuracy and efficiency are both crucial in item compromise detection, Zhang , Zhang and Li , Choe et al. , and Lee and Qian  framed the compromised item detection as a Phase II problem and utilized the moving-sample sequential testing procedure to monitor items in real time. Their methods are flexible and computationally manageable. In addition to identifying compromised items, their methods are also able to evaluate detection efficiency via the lag criterion. However, as pointed out in Liu et al. , the moving sample size in their methods may be challenging for practitioners to tune to reach optimal performance and this method may be less capable of flagging compromised items when items are leaked gradually. To address both gradual and abrupt leakage issues, Liu et al.  proposed a generalized linear model and monitored each item at the level of natural days (though it can be adjusted to other time units). Nevertheless, a close review of their simulation conditions reveals that the estimated probability that an examinee has item pre-knowledge ranges from .68 to 1.0, suggesting that more than a half to all of the incoming examinees have item pre-knowledge. When the pre-knowledge probability is low, according to the pattern of their simulation results, their method may not be as powerful.

Lastly, Lee et al. , Lee and Lewis , and Veerkamp and Glas , utilized the cumulative sum (CUSUM) procedure to monitor item performance. Veerkamp and Glas  entails item recalibration at each CUSUM time-point, making it less flexible to apply. Even though Lee et al.  and Lee and Lewis  do not require item recalibration, the CUSUM parameters (k, h) need to be carefully determined based on item parameters, sample sizes, and in-control average run length (ARL). While the literature on compromised item detection is still growing, none of the existing studies has addressed this problem via Bayesian approaches, such as Shiryaev's procedure (Shiryaev, ). Compared to frequentist approaches, the Bayesian approach to compromised item detection assumes unknown parameters as random variables instead of fixed, which allows (1) prior knowledge or expert inputs to be incorporated as additional information and (2) the uncertainty in parameter estimates to be characterized via the posterior distribution. In this study we address item compromise detection in a Bayesian change-point framework that combines both Phase I and Phase II detection. In Phase I detection we aggregate all response data and employ Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques to estimate potential item change-points and the post-change model. In Phase II detection, we utilize the Shiryaev procedure (Shiryaev, ) to monitor item performance in real time. According to Tartakovsky et al. , while the CUSUM procedure minimizes detection delay in the worst-case scenario across all possible values of the change-points (i.e., minimax optimality), the Bayesian Shiryaev procedure minimizes the posterior expected detection delay subject to a Type I error constraint. Under certain regularity conditions, the Shiryaev procedure achieves higher posterior detection efficiency.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. First, we introduce the Bayesian change-point framework for item compromise, where the responses deviate from the standard item response theory model once an item becomes compromised, resulting in a mixture of individuals with and without pre-knowledge. MCMC estimation of the Bayesian change-point model for finite-horizon data is discussed, followed by the Shiryaev procedure for Phase II (real-time) item compromise detection. The proposed method is then examined in simulations and on data generated according to an operational test: simulation I examines the change-point model, simulation II investigates the performance of the Shiryaev procedure with respect to latent ability estimates. The procedure was also examined on data generated based on an operational item pool and compared with the CUSUM (Lee & Lewis, ) procedure. Discussions about the proposed method and guidelines on how to employ the method are provided at the end.
BAYESIAN CHANGE-POINT DETECTION IN COMPROMISED ITEM DETECTION

The Bayesian change-point framework assumes that the distributions of data at each time-point differ before and after a specific time-point , namely, the change-point (Tartakovsky et al., ). Let  denote the last pre-change time-point, that is, the last administration (e.g., day) that an item remains uncompromised. For a particular item, the pre-change model  specifies the distribution of observed item responses prior to item compromise, for which a reasonable choice would be a standard item response model with pre-calibrated parameters. The post-change model, , on the other hand, specifies the distribution of observed responses after item compromise. To detect the change-point  in the Bayesian framework, the change-point  is treated as a discrete random variable. We assume a prior distribution for , denoted by , .

Depending on whether  can go to infinity, the change-point detection problem is either a Phase I problem, where response data are collected and analysed for a fixed number of time-points , or a Phase II problem, where new responses are collected in real time and are used to determine whether an item has become compromised. First, in the early stage of test administration, we gather response data from a fixed testing window, based on which we estimate the post-change model  and change-points of compromised items within this time-frame. With the post-change model  known, we apply the Shiryaev detection procedure to constantly monitor each item in the item pool in real time. Take a continuous test with a 200-item pool as an example. Our proposed method would utilize the response data collected from the first  test administration dates, say 30, to estimate the post-change model  and flag potential compromised items in the 30 days. The flagged items will then be replaced with new ones in future test administrations. From then on, the Shiryaev procedure will be applied at each time-point, to monitor each item in real time. We now formulate our method in detail below.
Phase I detection: Bayesian change-point model estimation

In this stage the response data from a fixed testing window are collected and used to estimate the post-change model; each item's change-point will also be estimated. For a given testing window across T time units, let  denote the latent abilities of the  examinees who took the test at time t. The response on item j from the ith examinee at time t is denoted by . When item j is not compromised, the pre-change model p 0 can be assumed to follow a standard item response model, such as the two-parameter logistic model whose item discrimination and difficulty parameters, respectively denoted by , are assumed to be pre-calibrated and known. On the other hand, while the item compromise process and mechanisms may not be as clear, a non-item-specific shift seems interpretable and parsimonious here. Phase II detection: Real-time detection through the Shiryaev procedure

With the post-change model  estimated, we can apply the Shiryaev procedure to monitor items in real time in future test administrations. The critical value  can be found using Monte Carlo inference. Recall that the goal is to detect a compromised item in a timely manner, while controlling the false detection rate (FDR) to a predetermined level. In sequential testing, a common method of Type I error control is via setting the average run length of the in-control process , to be greater than or equal to a threshold ,  is the expected time (in our case, days) until an in-control (i.e., uncompromised) item is falsely flagged as out of control (compromised). The threshold  is often pre-determined based on practical applications or statistical considerations such as controlling Type I error rates (e.g., Lee & Lewis, ; Ye et al., ). For instance, in Lee and Lewis , the threshold d was set to be the number of days of historically collected data. The critical value a can hence be estimated by simulating the stopping point of the Shiryaev procedure under the null (in-control) distribution.

We now present the algorithm for finding the critical value a. Similar to Ye et al. , this is identified using Monte Carlo simulation in conjunction with grid search. SIMULATION I: BAYESIAN CHANGE-POINT MODEL

The aim of simulation I is to examine the parameter recovery of the Phase I change-point model under a number of conditions. The Phase I model is a stationary model, in the sense that it monitors the responses of all items in the pool in a given testing window. For simplicity, we assume that the responses across time-points were collected from a test that implements a block planned missing design. Similar block designs are adopted in many educational tests (e.g., Beaton, ). Missingness induced from such designs are missing completely at random (MCAR). More specifically, a 200-item pool was considered in the current simulation. The first 100 items (set A) were used to assemble five disjoint test forms, each form consisting of 20 items. Similarly, the remaining 100 items (set B) were used to assemble another five forms of 20 items. At a given time-point, each examinee received one of the five forms from set A and another from set B. Thus, we have 5 x 5 = 25 test forms in total, each containing 40 items.
True parameter generation

Following the simulation design in Liu et al. , a 30-day testing window was considered. Within the 30-day window, the item pool remained unchanged, that is, no item replenishment or item removal was implemented. The number of examinees on each day, , was set to be either 500 or 1000. The latent ability of the examinees were drawn from the standard normal distribution. The item discrimination and difficulty parameters of each item were respectively generated from lognormal  and normal . The change-point of each item was generated from . As the testing window was set to 30, items whose change-point parameters were greater than 30 were capped at 30. According to this generation schema, if the true change-point parameter k of a given item was 30, this item remained uncompromised within this testing window. All the aforementioned parameter generation schemas are summarized in Table 1. In practice, as operational items are often pre-calibrated prior to test administration, discrimination and difficulty parameters were assumed known.

Evaluation criteria

The proposed model and the estimation algorithms were evaluated on chain convergence and parameter recovery. To evaluate MCMC chain convergence, we separately generated five chains with varying initial values. Each chain was run for 30,000 iterations. The convergence was assessed by monitoring the maximum of the Gelman-Rubin proportional scale reduction factor (PSRF; Gelman & Rubin, ). This statistic is calculated through the coda package in R (Plummer et al., ). At chain lengths ranging from 100 to 30,000, the PSRF was computed with the first half of the chain as burn-in; a PSRF lower than 1.1 suggests convergence.

To evaluate parameter recovery, post-burn-in posterior means (expected a priori [EAP]) of each parameter were first computed as point estimates. Recovery of continuous parameters (i.e., , , ) was assessed via average bias and root mean squared error (RMSE) between EAP estimates and true parameters. Let  and  respectively be the true value and EAP estimates of a parameter and N be the number of parameters. Likewise, the latent ability parameters were also well recovered. The impacts of the condition factors, , , and  were also manifestly consistent. The larger the sample size was on each day, the lower (or at least the more comparable) the RMSE and bias of the post-change model parameter estimates were. Similarly, the more examinees had pre-knowledge (i.e., higher ) or the more accurately those pre-knowledge examinees answered compromised items (i.e., higher ), the better the post-change model parameters were recovered. The sample size did not seem to affect latent ability estimates as the latter were mainly influenced by test length. Yet, the proportion of pre-knowledge examinees  negatively influenced the latent ability parameter estimates; the higher the value of , the worse (though slightly) latent ability estimates were recovered. This is expected: when more examinees had pre-knowledge on those compromised items, we had less information about the latent ability of these examinees as they were using their pre-knowledge to answer those compromised items instead of their true abilities, thereby increasing the overall RMSE of latent ability parameters. This pattern is even more manifest if we plot the bias and RMSE of latent ability estimates with respect to the number of compromised items examinees received, as shown in Figures 2 and 3. The more compromised items examinees received, the less accurate their latent ability estimates would be.

Next, we evaluated the parameter recovery of the change-point parameters. Overall, the change-point  can be estimated fairly accurately (i.e, absolute lag is less than ) if the sample size is large or  is high. The effect of condition factors on the recovery of  was consistent with continuous parameter estimates; the larger the sample size was on each day, the more accurate the  estimates were. Similarly, the more examinees had pre-knowledge and/or the more accurate those pre-knowledge responses were, the better the change-point parameters were estimated.

We further examined whether the proposed model was also able to distinguish compromised items from uncompromised items based on their change-point estimates. Across all conditions, most of the compromised items can be truly flagged by our model. But under some conditions (e.g., , , ), the Type I errors were very high. After scrutinizing the simulation results, we attributed such high Type I errors to the number of pre-knowledge examinees on each day after items become compromised. Even though the overall sample sizes were set to be either 500 or 1000 on each day in our simulation, the number of pre-knowledge examinees was not  due to our planned missing design. Based on this design, each item appeared in five forms while 25 test forms were randomly administered. Hence, on average, the number of pre-knowledge examinees on each day was in fact . Accordingly, the expected numbers of pre-knowledge examinees on each day for the three  conditions when  and  were respectively 15, 25, 35 and 30, 50, 70. When the sample size of pre-knowledge examinees was small, the estimates of the change-point was not as accurate. Nevertheless, when the number of pre-knowledge examinees increased (as shown in other simulated conditions), the Type I error dropped dramatically.

To further uncover the underlying pattern of the Type I error issue, we reviewed those falsely flagged uncompromised items within each condition. We used the 25th and 75th percentiles of the difficulty parameters to classify items into easy, medium, and hard items. Next, we plotted the proportion of falsely flagged items in each condition with respect to the three difficulty groups, as shown in Figure 4. According to this figure, in most conditions, easy items were more likely to be falsely flagged. This result is in fact consistent with what Lee and Lewis  found in their study; as most of the examinees had a higher probability of answering easier items correctly, distinguishing high chances of correct response due to pre-knowledge and due to relatively low item difficulty becomes challenging.

To summarize, simulation I showed that the proposed change-point model successfully converged within a short chain length, and the continuous parameters in the proposed model were recovered accurately. The recovery accuracy of the change-point parameters  depended on the number of pre-knowledge examinees on each day and the chance of correct response given pre-knowledge (i.e, magnitude of ). With a relatively large pre-knowledge group (e.g., sample size greater than 35) and , the change-point parameters can be accurately estimated. Based on these estimates, compromised items can be successfully detected.
SIMULATION II: REAL-TIME DETECTION WITH THE SHIRYAEV PROCEDURE

After the post-change model is estimated and becomes known, we can utilize the Shiryaev procedure to monitor each item individually and detect compromised items in real time. In this simulation, we aim to show how the Shiryaev procedure performed with latent ability EAP estimates in a number of conditions (the performance of Shiryaev procedure with true latent ability parameters is included in Appendix 2).

To begin with, we first removed the compromised items in the previous testing window and replenished the pool with new items. The item pool size remained 200. The true item parameters of new items were generated from the same distributions as in simulation I. The planned missingness design was again implemented where each examinee received one of 25 test forms. Next, we simulated the responses of a new 30-day testing window. Aligned with simulation I, 12 conditions were simulated. The prior of  in the Shiryaev procedure was set to be . In this simulation, each condition was replicated 1000 times and the results were averaged across all replications within each condition.
ARL of the Shiryaev procedure

Aligned with many other SQC procedures, such as CUSUM or Shewhart chart (e.g., Montgomery, ; Page, ), the goal of our detection procedure is to detect an item in a timely manner once it becomes compromised while controlling its FDR to a satisfactory level. To achieve this, as mentioned earlier, one can set the in-control ARL according to practical applications or statistical considerations.

In practice, as multiple items in the item pool are simultaneously monitored, multiple items are tested over repeated time-points. More often, practitioners may be concerned with controlling not only the FDR of each individual item across time (i.e., itemwise Type I error) but also the FDR of the entire item pool (i.e., poolwise Type I error) within a given time-frame. If the chosen threshold d for each individual item is too small, the poolwise FDR may be very high; yet if the threshold d is too large, the detection procedure may not be efficient at detecting compromised items promptly and have longer lags. Given that the determination of d may depend on a myriad of practical and statistical factors, instead of providing a one-size-fits-all solution for how to choose the threshold d, we set d to be 100 or 300 days in the current simulation study and chose the Shiryaev critical values accordingly. The corresponding poolwise Type I error rate and power are presented to illustrate how d can be chosen to achieve the desired balance between Type I and Type II errors.
Evaluation criteria

As the aim of real-time detection is to detect compromised items as soon as possible while controlling the false alarm rate, the evaluation criteria in this simulation include both detection accuracy and detection efficiency measures. The detection accuracy of the proposed procedure was measured by Type I error rates as well as power, whereas the detection efficiency was measured by the lag between the detection time and the true compromised time.

As indicated earlier, controlling the poolwise FDR is important in practice; the Type I error rate in our simulation is thereby defined as the FDR with respect to the entire item pool within a given time-frame (i.e., familywise Type I error; Zhang, ; Zhang & Li, ; Choe et al., ). The Type I error and power were computed in the same manner as simulation I, shown in equations (21) and (22).

passages.text: Moreover, the Shiryaev procedure showed good detection accuracy and efficiency in the presence of measurement error in ability. When we had large samples of pre-knowledge examinees or when those pre-knowledge examinees answered compromised items with high accuracy, the Shiryaev procedure was powerful in flagging compromised items within a short lag while controlling the poolwise Type I error. The compromised items can be detected in 5 days or less on average. We further investigated the items that failed to be flagged by the Shiryaev procedure. All these items became compromised in the last few days of the simulated testing window. In other words, the Type II error were likely to be caused by the censoring of the testing window size instead of the sensitivity of the detection procedure.

Finally, the effects of the simulation factors , ,  in this simulation were also consistent with what was found in simulation I. The more pre-knowledge examinees have and the more accurately they can answer those compromised items, the higher and the more efficient the detection power will be.

To sum up, with latent ability estimates being used, we examined the detection accuracy and detection efficiency of the Shiryaev procedure with respect to the two pre-determined ARL thresholds. The simulation results showed that the Shiryaev procedure was very sensitive in detecting compromised items and the compromised items can be detected in a fairly short time period. What is more, the results also confirmed our conjectures that a longer ARL threshold may lead to smaller poolwise Type I error rates but longer lags. The effects of the simulation factors were also found to be consistent with simulation I.
PERFORMANCE ON AN OPERATIONAL ITEM POOL

We further evaluated the performance of the proposed method and compared the Phase II Shiryaev procedure to the CUSUM method proposed in Lee and Lewis  under a realistic, high-stakes testing setting. Given that sequential testing data are rarely available for public use, we instead used the item parameter estimates from an operational test to generate the response data, similar to Choe et al. . The empirical data are the computer-based non-adaptive licensure test data found in Cizek and Wollack . The data include two test forms, each of which contains 170 operational items and 10 pilot items. We only used the 170 operational items in Form 2 in our analysis. Item-level responses were collected for all examinees. The sample size is 1644, where 48 possible cheaters as well as 61 compromised items were identified through rigorous application of data forensics methods. We used these labels as the true labels for items or examinees in our simulations.

As all these items are multiple-choice questions, we employed the three-parameter logistic model to calibrate item parameters and adapted the  and  response distributions in Phase I and Phase II detection accordingly. To avoid parameter contamination, we only included responses from examinees who were not flagged with pre-knowledge in item parameter calibration. DISCUSSIONS

In this study, we address the item compromise detection problem from a Bayesian change-point perspective. The method that we propose includes both Phase I and Phase II applications. In the early stage of test administration, we aggregated the response data and employed the Bayesian change-point model for the entire item pool across all accumulated time-points. Simulation I showed that the change-point model parameters can be accurately recovered, and parameter recovery depended on the number of pre-knowledge examinees, the difficulty of the item, and the chance of a correct response given pre-knowledge. If the sample size of pre-knowledge examinees is large or if they always answer compromised items correctly, the change-point parameters can be accurately estimated. On the other hand, differentiating compromised and uncompromised items becomes more challenging when items are easy or when the chance of correct response for those with pre-knowledge is low. With post-change model estimated, we can utilize the Shiryaev procedure in the later stages of test administration and monitor item performance in real time. Our simulations showed that the Shiryaev procedure is powerful in detecting compromised items with short lags, and the poolwise Type I error rate can be controlled to a satisfactory level. The operational pool example also showed the superior detection accuracy and efficiency of the Shiryaev procedure over CUSUM, under the simulation condition considered.

While the existing compromised item detection methods are either Phase I or Phase II applications, our method combining both applications may be superior in the sense of combining the strengths of both applications. In the early stage of test administration, item compromise may be less likely to occur than in later stages (Lee & Lewis, ; Zhang, ). Hence, in this stage, real-time detection may be computationally unnecessary; aggregating responses and employing the change-point model only once can identify compromised items and may not elicit substantially long detection lags. On the other hand, in later stages, when item compromise is more likely to occur, detection flexibility and efficiency become vital and Phase I detection may no longer fit. The Shiryaev detection procedure meets this requirement and can detect compromised items accurately and efficiently. Moreover, compared to other methods, the computation in our method is also straightforward. The only value that may need to be determined is the ARL in the Shiryaev procedure. As suggested earlier, this value should be set based on practical considerations as well as statistical concerns. If practitioners are only concerned about itemwise Type I error, the ARL of each item may be set as the testing window length or the number of test administrations, as Lee and Lewis  did in their simulation III. However, if poolwise Type I error is of more concern, the ARL may be chosen in a similar fashion to simulation II to achieve the desired level of poolwise Type I error rate within a time-frame. Last but not least, the Bayesian framework allows for incorporation of informative priors (e.g., for the change-point) to serve different practical needs. If Type I error (i.e., falsely flagging an uncompromised item) is more costly, a skewed prior for the change-point, such as the truncated geometric prior adopted in the operational test example, may be adopted. On the other hand, if Type II error (i.e., missing a compromised item) is more costly, a prior that places more mass on lower values of the change-point may be adopted. Also, as readers may tell from the model, when the change-point  is large, the marginal probability of pre-knowledge  will be low, and vice versa. Accordingly, practitioners may formulate the priors hierarchically.

One note about monitoring item performance in real time is how to choose the monitoring time unit. In our study as well as Liu et al. , items are monitored on a daily basis (though this can be adjusted to other time units) whereas Lee and Lewis  monitor items at the level of test administrations and Zhang , Zhang and Li , and Choe et al.  monitor item performance at the level of examinees. Depending on the item pool maintenance schedule, a balance should be kept between detection efficiency and computation costs. Real-time detection at the examinee level is of course efficient but also computationally expensive and possibly unnecessary. Given that items being detected may not be removed from the item pool right away, practitioners should choose this monitoring unit according to the nature of their specific tests, test item development progress, as well as the item pool removal and replenishment schedule.

Our proposed method also has several limitations. First, the Bayesian change-point model estimation is not fit for computerized adaptive testing (CAT) if item compromise occurs. CAT administers subsequent items based on the preliminary ability estimate from previously responded items. The sparsity in the observed responses is hence induced by missingness that is not completely at random. Whether the proposed procedures will be suitable for responses that are not MCAR should be studied in future research. The Phase I parameter estimation may also be computationally slow if the monitored item pool is incredibly large, in which case one alternative is to first partition the item pool into secure items and potentially compromised items and use those potentially compromised items only to calibrate the post-change model. Furthermore, for the proposed method, for modelling simplicity and statistical interpretations, we implicitly assume that the post-change model remains unchanged in the later stages of item administration. It is very likely that the probability of examinees having pre-knowledge  may increase monotonically in time. To resolve this issue, the Bayesian change-point model in Phase I detection may be estimated periodically or employing a more informative prior to update the post-change model. It can be used together with Shiryaev procedure to ensure both detection efficiency and detection accuracy in the later stages of test administration.

There are also multiple directions to extend the current study. This includes utilizing response times to remedy the issue that easy items tend to be falsely flagged as compromised items. With the inclusion of response times where time spent on an easy items might be shorter for examinees with pre-knowledge, the classification and detection are expected to be more accurate. Moreover, while all the existing methods monitor each item individually, the change-point model can also be extended by incorporating other covariates such as item overlaps. If an item is compromised due to overexposure or item theft, items that often appear on the same test forms with this compromised item may more likely to be compromised. Additionally, prior sensitivity analysis can also be conducted to examine how the prior in the Shiryaev procedure affects its performance. Furthermore, in Phase I detection, posterior point estimates (EAPs) of examinees' latent ability and the post-change model parameters were used. Future studies can explore whether the use of plausible values drawn from the posterior distribution, which capitalize on the uncertainty in parameter posterior distribution, can result in better performance of sequential detection procedures. A non-sequential implementation can be found in Chalmers and Ng . Finally, while the proposed method is aimed at detecting item compromise occurring in large-scale continuous tests, as remote learning and testing become increasingly relevant, future studies can also explore the adaptation of the methods here to address the item compromise issues in formative classroom assessments (Chang et al., ).

infons.authors: Zhang Q, Qian D, Tang DD, Liu J, Wang LY, Chen W, Wu CJ, Peng W

passages.text: Glabridin from Glycyrrhiza glabra Possesses a Therapeutic Role against Keloid via Attenuating PI3K/Akt and Transforming Growth Factor-beta1/SMAD Signaling Pathways.

Glabridin (Gla) is a typical flavonoid isolated from the Glycyrrhiza glabra with various bioactivities and is a common additive in many cosmetics. In our study, we evaluated the antiscarring effect of Gla from G. glabra in a rabbit ear hyperplastic scar model. Hematoxylin and eosin staining and Masson staining were applied to determine the pathological changes and collagen fibers of scar tissue in rabbits. The results suggested that Gla could reduce rabbit ear scar hyperplasia, inhibit inflammation, and decrease collagen production. Furthermore, the in vitro cell experiments were applied to determine the effects of Gla on human keloid fibroblasts (HKFs), and we observed that Gla suppressed the HKF cells' proliferation via inducing apoptosis. Subsequently, we found that Gla reduced collagen production in HKF cells. The further molecular mechanisms investigations suggested that Gla played a therapeutic role against keloid by attenuating PI3K/Akt and TGFbeta1/SMAD pathways. Our study would be beneficial for extending the applications of the known sweet plant of G. glabra.

infons.authors: Welsh J, Bak MJ, Narvaez CJ

passages.text: New insights into vitamin K biology with relevance to cancer.

Phylloquinone (vitamin K1) and menaquinones (vitamin K2 family) are essential for post-translational gamma-carboxylation of a small number of proteins, including clotting factors. These modified proteins have now been implicated in diverse physiological and pathological processes including cancer. Vitamin K intake has been inversely associated with cancer incidence and mortality in observational studies. Newly discovered functions of vitamin K in cancer cells include activation of the steroid and xenobiotic receptor (SXR) and regulation of oxidative stress, apoptosis, and autophagy. We provide an update of vitamin K biology, non-canonical mechanisms of vitamin K actions, the potential functions of vitamin K-dependent proteins in cancer, and observational trials on vitamin K intake and cancer.

infons.authors: Lee B, Choi GM, Hong JP, Cho DE, Kim Y, Yeom M, Han JJ, Kim SR, Hahm DH

passages.text: Menaquinone-7 ameliorates cerebrovascular calcification-associated memory decline in aged mice.

Menaquinone (MK)-7 is a vitamin K2 analog that functions as a cofactor of gamma-glutamyl carboxylase involved in the activation of vitamin K (VK)-dependent proteins. The present study aimed to evaluate the effect of MK-7 on memory and cognitive function in aged C57BL/6 mice. Eighteen-month-old mice were raised for a further 4 months, fed on a standard or calcium-rich diet (3 % [w/w]), and were orally given MK-7 (40 and 400 mug/day/mouse) five times per week during the same period. The Morris water maze (MWM) test was performed at 19 and 22 months. The aged mice showed noticeable memory declines in the MWM test at all time points compared with 6-week-old mice, and this memory loss was significantly restored by the daily administration of high-dose MK-7 for 4 months. MK-7 administration also improved micro-computed tomography-based cerebrovascular calcification and aging-associated declines in growth arrest-specific 6, total and carboxylated matrix Gla proteins, and ganglioside levels in the brain of aged mice. It serologically reduced phosphorous levels in the blood, but not the urea, cholesterol, and calcium. Taken together, the long-term administration of MK-7 significantly improved age-related memory and cognitive impairments, possibly through inhibition of cerebrovascular calcification in aged mice, indicating that it can be used to develop new drugs for improving memory and cognitive function in older adults.

infons.authors: Yang J, Imamura S, Hirai Y, Tsuchiya T, Tabata O, Kamei KI

passages.text: Gut-liver-axis microphysiological system for studying cellular fluidic shear stress and inter-tissue interaction.

To clarify the physiological and pathological roles of gut-liver-axis (GLA) in the human body, a GLA microphysiological system (GLA-MPS) holds great potential. However, in current GLA-MPSs, the importance of a physiologically relevant flow for gut and liver cells' cultivation is not fully addressed. In addition, the integration of individual organ perfusion, circulation flow, and organ tissue functions in a single device has not been achieved. Here, we introduce a GLA-MPS by integrating two cell-culture chambers with individually applied perfusion flows and a circulation channel with an on-chip pneumatic micropump under cell-culture chambers via a porous membrane for interconnecting them. We analyzed the fluid shear stress (FSS) with computational fluid dynamics simulations and confirmed that the physiologically relevant FSS could be applied to the gut (Caco-2) (8 x 10-3 dyn cm-2) and liver (HepG2) cells (1.2 x 10-7 dyn cm-2). Under the physiologically relevant flow, the Caco-2 and HepG2 cells in the GLA-MPS maintained a cell survival rate of 95% and 92%, respectively. Furthermore, the expression of functional proteins such as zonula occludens 1 (in Caco-2) and albumin (in HepG2) was enhanced. To demonstrate the GLA interaction, the inflammatory bowel disease was recapitulated by applying lipopolysaccharide for only Caco-2 cells. The inflammatory proteins, such as inducible nitric oxide synthase, were induced in Caco-2 and HepG2 cells. The presented GLA-MPS can be adapted as an advanced in vitro model in various applications for disease modeling associated with inter-tissue interactions, such as inflammatory disease.

infons.authors: Chuang KH, Yao RH, Jiang YN, Gui LX, Zheng SY, Lin MJ

passages.text: Attenuating effect of magnesium on pulmonary arterial calcification in rodent models of pulmonary hypertension.

OBJECTIVE: Vascular calcification has been considered as a potential therapeutic target in pulmonary hypertension. Mg2+ has a protective role against calcification. This study aimed to investigate whether Mg2+ could alleviate pulmonary hypertension by reducing medial calcification of pulmonary arteries. METHODS: Monocrotaline (MCT)-induced and chronic hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension rats were given an oral administration of 10% MgSO4 (10 ml/kg per day). Additionally, we administered Mg2+ in calcified pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) after incubating with beta-glycerophosphate (beta-GP, 10 mmol/l). RESULTS: In vivo, MCT-induced and chronic hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension indexes, including right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular mass index, and arterial wall thickness, as well as Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining-visualized calcium deposition, high calcium levels, and osteochondrogenic differentiation in pulmonary arteries, were mitigated by dietary Mg2+ intake. In vitro, beta-GP-induced calcium-rich deposits stained by ARS, calcium content, as well as the detrimental effects of calcification to proliferation, migration, and resistance to apoptosis of PASMCs were alleviated by high Mg2+ but exacerbated by low Mg2+. Expression levels of mRNA and protein of beta-GP-induced osteochondrogenic markers, RUNX Family Transcription Factor 2, and Msh Homeobox 2 were decreased by high Mg2+ but increased by low Mg2+; however, Mg2+ did not affect beta-GP-induced expression of SRY-Box Transcription Factor 9. Moreover, mRNA expression and protein levels of beta-GP-reduced calcification inhibitor, Matrix GLA protein was increased by high Mg2+ but decreased by low Mg2+. CONCLUSION: Mg2+ supplement is a powerful strategy to treat pulmonary hypertension by mitigating pulmonary arterial calcification as the calcification triggered physiological and pathological changes to PASMCs.

infons.authors: Murphy BM, Chen JZ, Rolo M, Eldam M, Jordan L, Sivananthan SJ, Kinsey R, Guderian JA, Pedersen K, Abhyankar M, Petri WA, Fox CB, Finlay WH, Vehring R, Martin AR

passages.text: Intranasal delivery of a synthetic Entamoeba histolytica vaccine containing adjuvant (LecA + GLA-3 M-052 liposomes): In vitro characterization.

Amebiasis, a disease caused by the parasite Entamoeba histolytica, is estimated to cause millions of infections and at least 55,000 deaths globally each year. With no vaccine currently available, there is an urgent need for an accessible means of stimulating protective mucosal immunity. The objective of this study was to characterize the nasal spray of a novel amebiasis vaccine candidate from a syringe-based liquid atomization device, the Teleflex MAD Nasal , in both adult and infant nasal airways. Human ergonomic testing was completed to determine realistic actuation parameters. Spray pattern, plume geometry, and droplet size distribution were measured to evaluate reproducibility of free plume characteristics. The Alberta Idealized Nasal Inlet (AINI) and three realistic infant nasal airways were used to determine the in vitro deposition profile in adult and infant airways, respectively. Collectively, in vitro results demonstrated the feasibility of delivering the vaccine candidate to target sites within the nasal airways. Penetration through the nasal airways that could lead to deposition in the lungs was below the limit of quantification for both adult and infant geometries, indicating a low likelihood of adverse events due to lung exposure. These results support continued investigation of intranasal delivery of the synthetic Entamoeba histolytica vaccine.
